abstract: A graph is biplanar if its edges split into two planar graphs. Paper 59 proved that a biplanar graph with independence number at most 3 has at most 28 vertices. We prove that 28 is impossible, so such graphs have at most 27 vertices. This closes the counting route $\chi\ge n/\alpha$ to ten colours for $\alpha\le3$; it does not decide whether biplanar graphs are 9-colourable. By hand and by imported theorems (Szeider; Papers 92 and 110 for degrees other than 10), a counterexample has a vertex $v$ of degree 10 whose non-neighbourhood $H$ has 17 vertices and $\alpha(H)\le2$. $H$ contains a spanning kernel $K$, the complement of a maximal triangle-free graph; 59,010 kernels arise. Four bounds of earth_moon_codex_two on the actual exterior ($|E(H)|\le82$, $|E(H)|\ne82$, and $K_8\subseteq H$ when $|E(H)|\in\{80,81\}$), proved with hand lemmas and DRAT-checked local models, discard all kernels with at least 82 edges by edge count. Of the remaining 244, 24 fail the $K_8$ condition, 14 are excluded by published theorems, and the rest reduce to 208 explicit 17-vertex graphs. Each is shown non-biplanar by a SAT model with lazily generated Kuratowski clauses; every certificate is checked in full, including drat-trim on every proof. No integer-programming, CP-SAT or sampled verdict is used. The supplement lists the kernels and the 208 graphs, checks the case analysis with standard-library code, and regenerates any certificate.
